title: Seeing Circles, Sines, and Signals: A Compact Primer on Digital Signal Processing
topics: Lesson 1, Introduction: the primer's visual, interactive, auditory, intentionally informal scope and its role as a companion rather than a sole DSP reference.
Lesson 2, Signals: continuous signals as quantities varying over time, illustrated by airplane altitude, temperature, and vehicle speed.
Lesson 3, Discrete Signals: periodic measurement, samples represented as zero-indexed lists, and the need to retain the sampling period alongside sample values.
Lesson 4, Sampling & Aliasing: multiple continuous histories consistent with the same samples, missed rapid events, and the information/cost tradeoff in sampling rate.
Lesson 5, Sound Waves: compression and rarefaction, frequency, wavelength, propagation speed, human hearing, and an interactive Web Audio sine oscillator.
Lesson 6, Timbre: fundamentals, harmonics, sine/square/saw/noise waveforms, two-second synthesized playback, and live spectrum analysis.
Lesson 7, Sine & Cosine: rotating phasors whose vertical and horizontal projections generate sine and cosine, with frequency and amplitude controls.
Lesson 8, Trigonometry Review: phase in degrees and radians, the unit circle, and cosine/sine as Cartesian coordinates.
Lesson 9, The Sampling Theorem: bandlimits, the greater-than-twice-bandwidth sampling condition, and interactive 1–4 Hz alias comparisons.
Lesson 10, Nyquist Frequency: a fixed 24 Hz sampler and the apparent reflected frequency as a sinusoid crosses 12 Hz.
Lesson 11, Wagon Wheel Effect: temporal sampling of rotation, apparent reversal or stasis, direction ambiguity, and an industrial-strobe safety connection.
Lesson 12, Sine Wave Aliasing: the family F+kFs of continuous sinusoids that agree at every sampling instant.
Lesson 13, Representations & Transforms: representations as tools for thought, Cartesian and polar coordinates, basis vectors, and the Fourier transform as a change of representation.
Lesson 14, The Fourier Transform: a DFT represented as harmonically related phasors chained tip-to-tail to synthesize a time-domain signal.
Lesson 15, Notation: a glyph-by-glyph unpacking of the DFT equation, including indexed input/output lists, exponentials, summation, and phase.
Lesson 16, Complex Numbers: multiplication by i as a 90-degree rotation and complex numbers expressed by real/imaginary components or magnitude/phase.
Lesson 17, Euler's Formula: exp(i phi)=cos(phi)+i sin(phi), the negative-exponent form, and decomposition of the DFT into cosine and negative-sine correlations.
Lesson 18, The Dot Product: multiply-and-sum arithmetic and its geometric interpretation as signed directional similarity.
Lesson 19, Correlation: dot products between a signal and phase-shifted sinusoids, including positive, zero, and negative correlation.
Lesson 20, Correlation With Sine: detecting a square wave's odd harmonics and exposing the failure of a sine-only detector for a component shifted by 90 degrees.
Lesson 21, Correlation With Sine and Cosine: two quadrature correlations encoded as one complex result whose magnitude is phase-independent.
Lesson 22, Discrete Fourier Transform Example: an animated eight-point DFT that displays every basis sample, product, sum, and complex output bin.
Lesson 23, Digging Deeper: interactive bin inspection, DC, the Nyquist bin, conjugate symmetry for real signals, and the effect of an input phase shift.
Lesson 24, Frequency Resolution: bin frequency kFs/N, spacing Fs/N, and the record-length versus latency tradeoff needed to resolve nearby tones.
Lesson 25, Zero-Padding: denser interpolation of the same spectrum without additional resolving information.
Lesson 26, Leakage: off-bin tones, finite rectangular observation, sidelobes, periodic-extension discontinuities, and windowing.
Lesson 27, Sine Wave Properties: orthogonality over a compatible full-period interval and closure of same-frequency sine-wave sums under arbitrary amplitude and phase.
Lesson 28, Using FFT Libraries: FFT output layouts, real-input packing, implementation-specific scaling, and a small Octave example.
Lesson 29, Conclusion: limits of the visual treatment and suggested continuations into convolution, autocorrelation, filtering, resampling, and phase-vocoder ideas.
key_results: Lessons 3–4: a sequence of sample values is not self-interpreting; its sampling period supplies the time axis, and no set of samples uniquely determines the continuous path between sample times without additional assumptions.

Lesson 4: a shorter sampling interval can rule out previously plausible aliases, but higher rates consume more storage and computation; undersampling can permanently discard events that occur between samples.

Lesson 5: frequency measures cycles per second, wavelength is inversely related to frequency at fixed propagation speed, and propagation speed depends on the medium rather than on the tone's frequency.

Lesson 6: timbre is tied to spectral composition: a sine has one component, an ideal square wave emphasizes odd harmonics, an ideal sawtooth contains integer harmonics, and noise spreads energy broadly and irregularly.

Lessons 7–8: sine and cosine are orthogonal projections of the same rotating unit phasor; changing amplitude changes its radius, changing frequency changes rotational speed, and changing phase changes initial angle.

Lesson 9: for a signal bandlimited to B hertz, the primer states that samples should be spaced by 1/(2B) seconds and the sampling rate should exceed 2B; equivalently, content at or above Fs/2 is not uniquely represented. Equality and endpoint behavior require care beyond the primer's informal wording.
Lessons 9–10: sampled frequency is observed modulo the sampling rate and reflected about Nyquist; at Fs=4 Hz, a 3 Hz sine produces the same samples as a sign/phase-reversed 1 Hz sine.

Lesson 11: temporal aliasing is not limited to audio—one sample per revolution makes a wheel look stationary, while sparse snapshots can reverse its apparent direction and can make rotating machinery deceptively dangerous.
Lesson 12: sinusoids whose frequencies differ by an integer multiple of Fs are indistinguishable at integer sample times, producing an infinite alias family around any sampled sinusoid.

Lessons 13–14: the DFT is a change from N time samples to N complex coefficients associated with harmonically related rotating phasors; chaining those phasors and tracing a projection reconstructs the represented periodic signal.

Lessons 15–17: Euler's identity turns each DFT kernel exp(-i phi) into cos(phi)-i sin(phi), revealing a real cosine dot product and an imaginary negative-sine dot product rather than an opaque complex exponential.

Lesson 18: the dot product is both multiply-and-sum arithmetic and a directional similarity measure: positive when vectors align, zero when perpendicular, negative when opposed, and largest in magnitude for strong alignment.

Lessons 19–21: correlation with only one sinusoidal phase can miss a matching component in quadrature; pairing cosine and negative-sine correlations produces a complex coefficient whose magnitude is insensitive to input phase while its angle records phase.

Lessons 20–21: the square-wave demonstration yields strong detector responses at the fundamental and odd harmonics; the response magnitude tracks the corresponding phasor radius in the constructed signal.

Lessons 22–23: an eight-point DFT uses eight basis frequencies; bin 0 is the constant/DC basis, bin 4 is the Nyquist-rate alternating basis, and bins above it mirror lower bins as conjugates for a real-valued input.
Lesson 23: a time shift changes DFT phases while preserving bin magnitudes in the demonstrated periodic setting; this makes magnitude-only spectra unable to determine signal alignment.
Lesson 24: DFT bin k corresponds to kFs/N and adjacent-bin spacing is Fs/N; genuinely finer discrimination requires a longer observation record, which increases latency.

Lessons 24–25: zero-padding increases N computationally and samples the underlying spectral curve more densely, but it does not lengthen the observed data or resolve two frequencies hidden by a short record.

Lesson 26: a sinusoid exactly centered on a DFT bin concentrates in that bin, while an off-bin sinusoid leaks across bins because finite truncation and periodic repetition introduce an endpoint mismatch.

Lesson 26: tapering with a Hann window smooths the record boundary and suppresses distant sidelobes at the cost of a wider main lobe and alteration of the data; windowing manages leakage rather than eliminating the resolution tradeoff.

Lesson 27: distinct integer-harmonic sinusoids are orthogonal over a compatible whole-period interval regardless of phase. This claim should not be generalized to arbitrary finite windows or arbitrary frequencies.
Lesson 27: any weighted sum of sinusoids at the same frequency is another sinusoid at that frequency, with amplitude and phase obtained by vector addition of the component phasors.

Lesson 28: FFT libraries compute the DFT with different storage layouts and normalization conventions, so users must distinguish full complex output, packed real output, and positive-frequency-only output and must read the library documentation.

Lesson 28 caution: the primer's N/2 scaling remark is heuristic and convention-sensitive, appropriate to some one-sided real-sinusoid amplitude interpretations but not a universal FFT/IFFT round-trip rule; an unnormalized forward/inverse pair normally needs an overall 1/N factor.
pedagogy: The primer is a tightly staged visual argument: it begins with everyday time-varying quantities, creates unease about what samples omit, makes sine and cosine physical through a rotating line, introduces alternative representations before notation, then reduces the DFT to dot products before animating every operation. Its strongest method is coordinated multiple representations—unit circle, waveform, sample dots, basis vector, product plot, number line, complex plane, phasor chain, and audio—updated together as a learner drags a small number of controls. Controls usually isolate one conceptual variable: sample rate, phase, amplitude, basis bin, input waveform, record length, zero count, or window. The DFT walkthrough offers Slow/Normal/Turbo pacing, while the deeper explorer adds Next/Previous Bin and Change Input, allowing both narrated and self-directed passes. Audio demonstrations connect abstract spectra to hearing, and concrete stories (an aircraft's missed descent, a reversing wheel, turbine power versus wind, a strobe near machinery) keep the stakes visible. The prose explicitly favors simplicity and fun over rigor and repeatedly invites experimentation; it supplies no formal exercises, assessments, derivations of sampling reconstruction, or production code. A course should therefore reuse its prediction-and-manipulation pattern but add checkpoints, equations with declared normalization, boundary conditions, and counterexamples. Specific statements needing instructor qualification are the strict/equality details of the Nyquist criterion, DC as an unnormalized sum rather than literally an average, orthogonality only over compatible integration/sample intervals, the schematic square/saw coefficients used by some animations, and the FFT scaling remark that mentions N/2 as though it were universal.
figures: Recreate the airplane-altitude sampling story as one smooth trajectory, sparse measurement dots, and four distinct between-sample paths; add a sample-period slider that makes the rapid 60–70 minute descent appear or disappear. [Lessons 2–4]
Build a listen-and-see oscillator with click/drag frequency control on a perceptual scale, Play/Mute, a phasor/wave trace, and contextual bands for hearing, speech, and piano fundamentals. [Lesson 5]

Recreate the timbre laboratory with sine, square, sawtooth, and noise buttons, synchronized two-second playback, waveform view, and live magnitude spectrum; allow a 440 Hz anchor and harmonic labels. [Lesson 6]
Link a rotating phasor to simultaneous sine and cosine traces, with amplitude and frequency sliders and colored horizontal/vertical projections. [Lessons 7–8]

Recreate the four-wave alias explorer: switch among 1, 2, 3, and 4 Hz continuous waves while a sample-rate slider controls shared sample dots; explicitly prompt learners to predict which curves become indistinguishable. [Lesson 9]
Animate a tone rising through a fixed 24 Hz sampler while a second curve shows the apparent frequency folding downward after the 12 Hz Nyquist boundary. [Lesson 10]

Build a wagon-wheel/stroboscope simulation with rotation speed, sampling-flash rate, frozen snapshot trail, and displayed apparent angular velocity; include a prominent real-world machinery safety warning. [Lesson 11]
Show a 1 Hz sinusoid sampled at 6 Hz alongside aliases at 1+k·6 Hz, with shared sample dots and an integer-k control that progressively reveals the infinite alias family. [Lesson 12]

Create a representation-switcher for one point: Cartesian coordinates and orthogonal basis vectors on one side, radius/angle and rotation on the other, followed by a matching time-domain/frequency-domain switch for one signal. [Lesson 13]
Recreate the five-harmonic synthesis demo with amplitude sliders, rotating phasors chained tip-to-tail, and the endpoint's vertical projection drawing the resulting waveform. [Lesson 14]
Turn the DFT formula into a progressive annotation: selecting a glyph highlights its semantic role, then expands exp(-i phi) into paired cosine and negative-sine basis plots. [Lessons 15–17]
Build a draggable two-vector dot-product scene tied to elementwise products, their sum, and a signed number line; snap to parallel, perpendicular, and antiparallel cases. [Lesson 18]

Recreate the turbine-correlation example as a phase slider over two traces, a signed product-area plot, and a moving dot-product indicator, so positive, zero, and negative correlation are visible at once. [Lesson 19]

Build a frequency detector for the same square-like input with a sine-only mode and a sine-plus-cosine mode; let phase rotate while the complex result circles at constant radius, exposing why quadrature is necessary. [Lessons 20–21]

Recreate the complete eight-point DFT animation with selectable sine/square/saw inputs, Slow/Normal/Turbo controls, and a step ledger for basis samples, products, real/imaginary sums, and each output bin. [Lesson 22]

Create a DFT bin microscope with Previous/Next Bin, Change Input, and phase controls; coordinate input, cosine/sine basis, products, complex coefficient, DC, Nyquist, and conjugate-pair highlighting. [Lesson 23]
Compare two aligned record-length panels for a 5+6 Hz signal: the short record merges the tones and the long record separates them, with Fs/N and observation latency updated numerically. [Lesson 24]

Make a two-row zero-padding demonstration: first append zeros to eight fixed informative samples and show a denser but unchanged spectral envelope; then add genuine measured samples and show actual separation of two nearby components. [Lesson 25]

Build a leakage explorer with a 1–3 Hz off-bin frequency slider, rectangular versus Hann window toggle, loop-boundary preview, and linked raw, windowed, and zero-padded spectra; annotate main-lobe width and sidelobe suppression. [Lesson 26]

Recreate the FFT-library layout comparison as one labeled mapping from a real time sequence to full complex, conjugate-symmetric, packed-real, and positive-only arrays, with a normalization selector for common conventions. [Lesson 28]
gems: The instruction not to connect sampled dots is a compact antidote to a common beginner illusion: a drawn interpolating line silently adds information that the sampler never observed. [Lesson 4]
The airplane example makes aliasing consequential without starting from a sinusoid: a serious descent between ten-minute reports can vanish completely from the recorded sequence. [Lessons 3–4]
At four samples per second, the 3 Hz trace appears as a vertically flipped 1 Hz trace, a particularly clean visual bridge from ambiguity to spectral folding. [Lesson 9]
The 24 Hz Nyquist animation pairs an increasing true frequency with a descending reflected alias, turning a static rule into a memorable crossing event. [Lesson 10]
The wagon-wheel lesson carries the sampling idea into physical safety: a strobe can make dangerous rotating machinery look stationary. [Lesson 11]
The primer pauses before Fourier analysis to compare 389 in Arabic and Roman numerals and invokes the idea that a representation can be a decisive intellectual tool. [Lesson 13]
Five draggable harmonic amplitudes control both a chain of rotating phasors and its traced projection, making synthesis appear before the DFT is dissected. [Lesson 14]
Multiplication by i is taught as a literal quarter-turn repeated four times, making complex arithmetic spatial before it becomes algebraic. [Lesson 16]
The dot-product explorer unifies the arithmetic recipe with geometry: the same value moves continuously from maximum positive through zero to maximum negative as one vector rotates. [Lesson 18]

A sine-only detector is deliberately allowed to fail when the target component is shifted by 90 degrees; the failure creates the need for the cosine channel rather than merely asserting it. [Lessons 20–21]
The eight-point walkthrough exposes every multiply and add and lets the learner alter both waveform and animation speed, an unusually literal executable explanation of the DFT. [Lesson 22]
The deeper DFT explorer makes three special structures inspectable rather than decorative: the constant DC basis, the alternating Nyquist basis, and conjugate mirror bins. [Lesson 23]

The zero-padding chapter uses fixed informative samples against appended zeros, then contrasts that with a genuinely longer observation—the exact comparison needed to defeat the 'more FFT points means more information' misconception. [Lesson 25]

The leakage explanation closes the finite record into a loop so the endpoint discontinuity becomes visible before introducing a Hann taper; the window therefore solves a seen boundary problem rather than arriving as a formula. [Lesson 26]
The conclusion openly warns that visual explanations can mislead and asks readers to report misconceptions, a useful model for presenting intuitive DSP material with epistemic humility. [Lesson 29]
chapter_map: Introductory motivation, continuous/discrete signals, sampling ambiguity, sound, and timbre → Part 1, lessons 1–6.
Phasors, trigonometric coordinates, sampling theorem, Nyquist folding, temporal aliasing, and sine alias families → Part 2, lessons 7–12.
Representations, Fourier synthesis, DFT notation, complex-plane geometry, and Euler decomposition → Part 3, lessons 13–17.
Dot products, correlation, quadrature detection, the complete eight-point DFT, and bin-level structure → Part 4, lessons 18–23.
Frequency resolution, zero-padding, leakage and windows, sine identities, FFT-library conventions, and next steps → Part 5, lessons 24–29.
